questions.stem: A child has jerk nystagmus OS with a large left head turn. Which Fresnel prism option would reduce the head turn?

options.A: Base in OD, base in OS
options.B: Base out OD, base out OS
options.C: Base in OD, base out OS
options.D: Base out OD, base in OS

questions.explanation: To reduce a head turn in a child with nystagmus, orient the prisms so their apices point toward the null zone; this shifts the image into the null zone. Here the null zone is in right gaze, so the prism over the right eye should be base-in and the prism over the left eye base-out. Surgical correction of a head turn instead rotates the eyes away from the null point.
questions.compilerNote: The compiler's lettering differs from the exam screenshot pasted beside it, where the same content is option D. The content matches; the letter here is the compiler's. Marked as a duplicate.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is referred from paediatrics after being diagnosed with Usher syndrome based on hearing loss and vestibular findings. On examination you found an exotropia of 35 prism dioptres. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
questions.explanation: The exotropia is most likely sensory, and what follows depends on the type of Usher syndrome; Cogan syndrome is also in the differential. Usher syndrome is the association of retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. Of its three types, type 1 has early profound deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, an extinguished ERG and vestibular areflexia; type 2 has moderate to severe hearing loss from birth with retinitis pigmentosa developing in the second decade and normal vestibular function; type 3 has progressive hearing loss with variable retinitis pigmentosa and sporadic vestibular function. Cogan syndrome is a rare systemic autoimmune vasculitis with intraocular inflammation and vestibuloauditory dysfunction developing within months of each other.
questions.compilerNote: The compiler wrote the answer as "C (ERG is better)" — they accepted the recalled key while noting an electroretinogram would be the more useful test. Marked as a duplicate.

questions.stem: A child has unilateral retinoblastoma and both parents are normal. What is the chance of a sibling having retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation: With unaffected parents and a unilaterally affected child, the risk to a sibling is very low, under a few percent. On the AAO inheritance chart it is quoted as under 1%, which among these choices is closest to 1-2%. The risk rises to about 5% where the affected child's disease is bilateral, and to 45% where a parent is a carrier.

questions.stem: A picture shows a large orbital floor fracture. What is the management?
questions.explanation: In cases of severe entrapment — a complete lack of supraduction, fairly severe pain on eye movement, or haemodynamic instability — urgent intervention is warranted. Most cases with less severe dysmotility resolve without intervention, so it is prudent to wait at least 14 days to repair an isolated orbital floor fracture, especially if motility improves in the first week. A fracture involving more than 50% of the orbital floor, or combined with the medial wall, is an indication for repair within 1 to 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A picture shows a lower lid lesion excision involving less than one third of the lid. How would you repair it?
questions.explanation: Since the defect is under 33%, the answer is primary closure. Direct closure is used for defects less than 33% of the lid width. For defects involving 33 to 50%, the eyelid can be freed with a lateral canthotomy and a semicircular Tenzel flap rotated into the defect. The Cutler-Beard procedure is used for upper eyelid defects greater than 50% of the lid width, and lower lid defects greater than 50% are repaired with a modified Hughes procedure.

questions.stem: Orbital cellulitis with a black eschar on the nose. What is the organism?
questions.explanation: A black eschar is a sign of mucormycosis. Invasive fungal sinusitis, also known as phycomycosis or mucormycosis, is the most common and most virulent fungal disease involving the orbit. It shows non-septated, large, branching hyphae with invasion of blood vessels, thrombosis and necrosis, and a black eschar may be visible in the nose or palate. Intracranial spread is haematogenous via the ophthalmic artery. Risk factors are diabetes mellitus in 70%, immunosuppression in 18%, renal disease in 5% and leukaemia in 3%. Treatment requires immediate and emergent surgical debridement, intravenous amphotericin B and control of the underlying illness.

questions.stem: A carotid-cavernous fistula after trauma arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: A direct, high-flow carotid-cavernous fistula follows trauma and arises from a tear in the intracavernous internal carotid artery. Indirect, low-flow fistulas instead arise from dural branches and are usually spontaneous.
